chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 2 of 6): the poet confesses his bondage to women, many of them named as selling themselves for money, and to the body as a hut of guts and blood that ends on the bier, and asks for Murugan's feet, his company of devotees, and his coming on the peacock when Death's messengers arrive; the praise turns on the hunter girl, the vel against Sura, Vishnu as uncle and Murugan as Siva's teacher.
structure_note: Courtesan and lust songs (37, 39 to 41, 43 to 45, 47, 49, 50), the body and death (38, 42, 46, 48), and two self-accusing pleas (36, 40). 41, 42 and 49 are in a dense chiming rhythm of short syllables that is hard to divide; 43 gives its praise to Krishna's flute; 48 ends on சூராந்தகனே, not பெருமாளே.

36.reading: The poet heaps names on himself, one who joined women with arrow-like eyes, faulty, a fool who keeps to no path, base, wasted, wholly ignorant, dull, sick with diseases wrapped in great deeds, without truth, and asks Murugan not to scorn him but to give him one day his cool feet with jewelled anklets so that he may have a life. The praise names the leader on the peacock who sought out and joined in the forest the hunter girl of whom Narada spoke, the little son of the Devi, the supreme mother with honeyed speech, at Thiruchiralaivay (Senthil) under its high groves.
36.nuance: The plea is almost entirely a list of accusative self-names (ஏதனை மூடனை ... ஈனனை வீணனை ... ஏழையை மோழையை ... வாய்மையிலாதனை), each one the object of இகழாதே, 'do not scorn'. ஏடெழுதா முழு ஏழை may mean one who cannot write a single leaf, i.e. unlettered. Narada (நாரதனார் புகல் குறமாதை) is named as the one who told of Valli.

37.reading: In a run of clipped two-syllable words the poet speaks of wandering women who, without thinking or looking, come with their charms until life faints, sulk as if without goodness and give an unreachable delusion, and asks not to be shaken within by them but to be given grace without Murugan's word swerving. The praise names the unbeaten warrior who pierced the hill, the vel that made deceitful Sura flee to the eight directions, the one dear to the konrai-wearing father who rides the bull, and the sweet-spoken son easy to his lovers, at Senthil.
37.nuance: எட்டாமால் தந்திட்டு உழல்மாதர்: the women give a delusion (மால்) that cannot be reached or ended. The plea நின்சொல் கோடாது என் கைக்கு அருள் தாராய் may ask that the Lord's promise not bend; the clipped rhythm makes most of the first half hard to divide.

38.reading: The poet pictures the end: beauty gone, the body slack, the senses fail and it becomes a corpse; some lift the bier, great drums beat in order, the children follow rolling on the ground, and then leave it on the road; he asks whether he will escape this false life and know how to reach Murugan's feet. The praise is a battle scene: Krauncha split, the sea dried, the demons' crowns falling, headless trunks and vultures dancing in pools of blood, and Murugan at Senthil who saw the fruit of the knowledge of the true faith.
38.nuance: மித்தை is mithya, the false or unreal: the whole sequence of death and mourning is named as the illusion to escape. கிடஞ்சம் கிடஞ்சம் is the drum's own sound. சற்சமய வித்தைப் பலன் கண்டு, 'having seen the fruit of the learning of the true religion', may refer to Murugan's victory over other faiths.

39.reading: The poet confesses calling women's speech sugar-candy, their waists creepers and their eyes arrows and poison, and living night and day under their sway, burning in old deeds by fate; he asks Murugan, seeing him fall, to give his lotus feet and come saying 'fear not, fear not', so that he may join the loving devotees who sing his praise and gain their nature. The praise names the jewelled chest that the hunter girl embraced, the one who, seeing the gods' plea for refuge, rode the peacock to war, conquered the demons, married on the hill and came to Senthil.
39.nuance: The remedy asked is company: பண்புடைய சிந்தை யன்பர் தங்களினுடன் கலந்து பண்புபெற, to mix with devotees and so take on their nature. விதியாலே பண்டைவினை கொண்டு names both fate and old deeds as the force behind his bondage. குன்றிடை மணம் புணர்ந்து may be the marriage to Devayanai on a hill.

40.reading: The poet asks not to be deluded by women whom even Lakshmi cannot equal, with sandal on their breasts, eyes skilled in stealth and fragrant dark hair, but to reach a pure mind, learn and understand virtue, wealth and pleasure fully, and having left them, know grace itself; for this he asks the feet with ringing anklets. The praise is a long litany of the Goddess (Kumari, Kali, Sankari, Gauri, Ambika, Kundali, Uma) and of Ganapati with the mouse, and names Murugan as the younger brother whom the moon-crowned Siva delights in, at Senthil of plantain, turmeric and ginger.
40.nuance: அறம் பொருள் இன்பமும் அடைய ஓதி உணர்ந்து தணந்தபின் அருள்தானே அறியுமாறு: the three aims of life are to be learnt fully and then left, and only then is grace known, an order that sets the Lord's grace above and after the three. The Goddess's names include குடிலை and குண்டலி, Tantric names of her power.

41.reading: The poet describes women with breasts like elephant tusks and golden pots, swinging earrings and conch-like throats, whom he calls women for hire, who tire, then laugh, call a man and feign longing, and asks whether he must wander here suffering for their breasts. The praise names the vel that crushed the demons and broke the hill while the gods praised, the one who gives his devotees the virtue of the bowed head, the joined hands, the kadamba garland, Siva and austerity, and the lord at Senthil who sleeps on the breasts of the hunter girl and of Indra's daughter.
41.nuance: சம்பளமாதர், 'women of wages', names the courtesans as paid, and சண் பசப்பும் is their feigned pallor of love. சிரப்பண்பும் கரப்பண்பும் ... சிவப்பண்பும் தவப்பண்பும் தருவோனே: Murugan gives the marks of worship of head and hands as well as inner qualities. The chiming short-syllable rhythm makes many divisions uncertain.

42.reading: The poet speaks of the womb-born body of blood and sores, melted by women whom he follows, mingles with, quarrels with and is tangled with, reeling, until Yama comes with his staff and the world takes fright and he dies; he asks Murugan to see his confusion, save him, break the prison of the body of birth, and give the joy of his feet. The praise names the bright vel that killed the demon in the clear sea where the sun moves, Kumaresa at Senthil where waves cast up conches, the son of Sankari, of Sankara and of Ganga, who sleeps on the hunter girl's breasts.
42.nuance: பிறப்பங்கம் சிறைப்பங்கம் சிதைத்து: the body given by birth is a prison to be broken, not reformed. Ganga is named as one of his parents (கங்கையட்கும் சுதன்), from the story of Siva's sparks carried to the reed pool. The middle lines (செருத்தண்டம் தரித்தண்டம் ...) are hard to divide.

43.reading: The poet describes the courtesans: breasts flowing with sandal, eyes of poison mixed with nectar, quarrelsome with anyone, leading moneyless youths astray and leaving them spent, mocking all in the street, giving love by exactly the measure of the money, melting in bed for great wealth, ready to embrace even a corpse, drunk on liquor; he asks for grace to leave all ties with them. The praise is a picture of Krishna's flute, at whose music the tiger cub drinks the cow's milk and the calf the tigress's, mountains melt, dry trees sprout and birds come down, and names Murugan the nephew who delights that cloud-dark one, at the shore of Senthil.
43.nuance: பிளவு பெறில் அதில் அளவளவு ஒழுகியர்: given a scrap, they give just that much. பிணமும் அணைபவர், 'they would embrace even a corpse', turns the courtesan's indifference into an image of death. The Krishna passage, with its reversal of nature (கழை = flute, ஏழ் தொளை = seven holes), is the longest single myth in these songs and is given to Vishnu, not Murugan.

44.reading: The poet describes women born to name their price, hair loosened, eyes reddened, hands joined, hearts melting, joining with seeming love, friendship and kindness, uniting, tiring and mingling again, and asks whether he must forever suffer wandering so. The praise names the vel given by the dark-throated Siva who opened his eye and burnt Kama, Murugan the friend of devotees who fought the deceivers, the nephew of Rama whose arrow burnt the heads of Lanka's king, and Kandha who came to Senthil in red anklets.
44.nuance: பிறந்து விலைகூறி: the women are 'born to quote a price', and the love, friendship and kindness (அன்பு நண்பு பண்பு) they show are part of the sale. The praise sets Siva burning Kama (அனங்கன்) beside the plea against lust.

45.reading: The poet speaks of women whose eyes defeat the young deer, with lotus-bud breasts and night-dark hair, who bargain to strip a man of all his wealth and make him trust them, and asks Murugan to look with grace on one who, playing with them, wastes away like a frog that has eaten poison. The praise names Kumaresa, the guru, who rode the peacock with the red-eyed serpent in its beak and killed the demon army, at Senthil of areca, coconut and ponds where monkeys dance.
45.nuance: நன்று பொருள் தீர என்று விலை பேசி: the bargaining is aimed at the man's wealth running out. நஞ்சுபுசி தேரை: the frog that has eaten poison and wastes away is a fresh image for the lover.

46.reading: The poet asks that before Death's cruel messengers bind his feet with the noose and drag him off, and before loving sons and mothers follow wailing to the burning ground, Murugan come before him on the peacock, with trident, sword, club, red cock, bow, shoulders, chest and pure anklets, so he may see him with longing. The praise names Vishnu, who gave nectar to the gods when they feared the poison Siva took and who sleeps on the roaring sea, as his uncle, and Murugan the life of Senthil who hurled the vel so that Sura fell.
46.nuance: The plea is for sight at the hour of death (காண ஆர்வம் செயும்), and it lists the Lord's weapons and body one by one as what he wants to see. The cock (சேவல்) appears here among the weapons, as the banner.

47.reading: The poet confesses bowing to women, sinking in the pool of the navel, drinking the nectar of lily lips, and drowning in a sea of pleasure among those with cloud-dark hair and breasts scented with aloe and camphor, and asks Murugan gently to bring him to shore and give his golden anklets. The praise names him the one who told the one thing to Siva, whose measure Brahma could not find and who bathes in Ganga reaching to the sky's sphere, and the lord of Senthil where waves throw pearls onto towers, walls and streets.
47.nuance: The plea uses the sea of births image (இன்பக் கடலூடே அமிழுவேனை ... கரைசேர்த்து) for the sea of pleasure. கம்பர்க்கு ஒன்றைப் புகல்வோனே is the teaching of Siva (here as கம்பர், the lord of Kanchi), though Om is not named. The opening, குகர மேவு மெய்த் துறவினின் மறவா, seems to set the true renunciation of cave-dwellers against the poet's bowing to women, but its sense is unclear.

48.reading: The poet calls his body a rough hut of guts, fat, bone, water, filth, blood, nerves, pus and flesh wrapped in skin, which he carries about with fondness, wearying himself among women whose dark eyes are Kama's arrows until his understanding fails, and asks Murugan to remove that nature, give his paired feet and rule him. The praise names Murugan the lord of Senthil on whose arms the hunter girl lives, who circled the world on the peacock, who took up the vel in one hand to pierce the hill, and the destroyer of Sura who stood in the sea.
48.nuance: The list குடர் நிணம் என்பு ... குருதி நரம்பு ... தோல் is the stock anatomy of disgust, set against the poet's own fondness (குனகி மகிழ்ந்து) for this hut. The song ends on சூராந்தகனே, 'ender of Sura', without the usual பெருமாளே.

49.reading: The poet speaks of women with sandal and kumkum on their breasts and red carp eyes that call, and of himself toiling in the sorrowful pot of the body, eating and enjoying until the body-lump grows fat, and asks not to wander so but to be joined to the red feet with bells brighter than the rising sun. The praise names Siva with konrai on his golden hair, Sankari who shares his side, Murugan whose strong arms delight the elephant's daughter and the deer's daughter, and the lord at Senthil where conches roll from the sea.
49.nuance: உடற்பிண்டம் பருத்து: the body fattened by feasting is the image of waste. குஞ்சரக் கொம்பும் கலைக் கொம்பும் appear to be Devayanai, raised by the elephant, and Valli, born of a doe. Like 41, the song is in a chiming short-syllable rhythm and many divisions are guesses.

50.reading: The poet describes women with shaking breasts, bangles, bee-haunted hair, voices like cuckoos and parrots and eyes like fish, who infatuate even the vidyadharas, and asks that he, suffering in sickness and thoughts of birth, be ruled so as to reach Murugan's shining feet. The praise is a battle with drums and conches in which the Suras fall and the sea burns at the vel's smile, and names Murugan the king in whom the Vedas delight as the guru Sankara loved, who delights in the hunter girl at Senthil praised by Sambhu.
50.nuance: சங்கரன் உகந்த பரிவின் குரு எனும் சுருதி: the Vedas themselves call him the guru Siva loved, a reference to the teaching myth without naming Om. The song ends on தம்பிரானே rather than பெருமாளே.

links.note: Both bring a corpse into the courtesan's bed: in the Kural the man embracing her is embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; in 43 it is she who would embrace even a corpse for money.

Both list the body's insides, guts, blood, bone, sinews and skin, almost word for word (குடர், குருதி, என்பு, நரம்பு, தோல்). The Naladiyar turns the list on the desired woman; 48 turns it on the poet's own body, which he still fondles.

Both follow the drums of a funeral to the moment the body is left: the Naladiyar ends with the dying carrying the dead; 38 ends with the mourners leaving it on the road, and calls the whole scene mithya, a false life to escape.
Both ask Murugan to come on the peacock at the hour when Death's men arrive with the noose; 46 adds the kin following to the burning ground and asks above all to see his form.

source_issues: Song 47: corrupt character in கடலு஡டே (line 7), probably கடலூடே; the CORRUPT_CHARS field flags it. Also தட்முழ்கி (line 2), probably தடமூழ்கி, unflagged.
Song 39: unflagged garble மிக்முழ்கி (line 10), probably மிகமூழ்கி; the source seems to write ்மு for மூ here and in 47.
Song 48 ends சூராந்தகனே and song 50 தம்பிரானே rather than பெருமாளே; this is the text, not an error, but the shrine is named only within the praise.
